title: Paediatric Intensive Care
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Intensive care for children provides organ‑supportive treatment for life‑threatening illness or injury. In low‑resource settings clinicians must prioritize rapid assessment, simple bedside tools and pragmatic escalation.

sections.p: Paediatric intensive care is the provision of advanced monitoring and organ‑support (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, neurologic) for children whose condition is unstable or deteriorating despite standard ward care.
b: Requires a dedicated high‑dependency area with trained staff
Diagnosis is clinical – failure of at least one vital system or need for invasive support

sections.p: Severity is gauged by organ‑failure scores (e.g., PELOD‑2) and by the need for invasive interventions.
b: Mild: single organ dysfunction, no invasive ventilation
Moderate: two organ systems or need for non‑invasive ventilation
Severe: three or more organ failures or need for invasive ventilation/vasopressors

sections.p: In East African and similar low‑resource hospitals the common precipitants are infections, severe malaria, sickle‑cell crises, and trauma.
b: Severe pneumonia (bacterial, viral, TB)
Malaria with cerebral involvement or severe anaemia
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis or acute chest syndrome
Sepsis from Gram‑negative bacteraemia, HIV‑related opportunists
Traumatic head injury, burns, or foreign‑body airway obstruction

sections.p: Children arrive with altered consciousness, respiratory distress, shock, or oliguria. Look for rapid breathing, grunting, cyanosis, capillary refill >2 s, and a falling Glasgow Coma Scale.
b: Respiratory failure: tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, SpO₂ < 90 % on room air
Circulatory shock: tachycardia, weak pulses, cold extremities, MAP < 65 mmHg
Neurologic compromise: seizures, GCS ≤ 8, pupils unequal

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on bedside signs (e.g., capillary refill for perfusion, respiratory pattern for ventilation) and treat empirically.

t.b: Is oxygenation adequate? → SpO₂ < 90 % indicates need for supplemental O₂ or ventilation
Is hypoglycaemia contributing? → < 2.5 mmol/L needs rapid glucose
Is there severe anaemia or leukocytosis? → Hb < 5 g/dL may need transfusion; WCC > 20 × 10⁹/L suggests bacterial sepsis
Is malaria present? → Any parasitaemia in a sick child warrants antimalarial therapy
Are kidneys failing? → Creatinine > 150 µmol/L or rising indicates AKI, consider dialysis if available
Is there pneumonia, pleural effusion, or pulmonary oedema? → Guides antibiotics and ventilation strategy
Is tissue hypoperfusion present? → Lactate > 2 mmol/L suggests shock, need for fluids/vasopressors

sections.p: Uncontrolled shock, refractory hypoxia, severe metabolic acidosis, and multi‑organ failure rapidly increase mortality.
b: Persistent MAP < 65 mmHg despite 40 mL/kg fluid bolus
SpO₂ < 85 % on maximal O₂
Lactate > 4 mmol/L after initial resuscitation
New arrhythmia or cardiac arrest

sections.p: First stabilise airway, breathing and circulation; then treat the underlying cause while providing organ support.
b: Airway: head‑tilt‑chin‑lift, suction, consider endotracheal intubation if GCS ≤ 8 or SpO₂ < 90 % on O₂
Breathing: give high‑flow O₂; if PaO₂ < 60 mmHg or work of breathing severe, start bag‑valve‑mask ventilation then invasive ventilation
Circulation: 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus; repeat once if shock persists; start noradrenaline infusion if MAP < 65 mmHg after fluids
Antibiotics: broad‑spectrum (e.g., ceftriaxone + gentamicin) within 1 hour for suspected sepsis; adjust for local resistance
Antimalarials: IV artesunate for severe malaria; follow with ACT
Blood transfusion: packed RBCs if Hb < 5 g/dL or symptomatic anaemia
Sickle‑cell crisis: IV fluids, analgesia, consider exchange transfusion if acute chest syndrome
Monitoring: hourly vitals, urine output, mental status, and lactate

sections.p: After stabilisation, step‑down to high‑dependency or ward when organ support is weaned. Prevent recurrence with vaccination, malaria prophylaxis, sickle‑cell education, and early sepsis recognition.
b: Vaccinate against pneumococcus, Hib, measles, and influenza
Provide insecticide‑treated nets and prompt malaria treatment
Educate families on sickle‑cell crisis triggers

sections.p: Paediatric high‑dependency unit (HDU) care, which provides non‑invasive monitoring but lacks invasive ventilation or vasopressor capability.
b: HDU: no mechanical ventilation, limited vasoactive support
ICU: full invasive organ support

sections.p: In severe malaria, peripheral parasitaemia may be low despite high parasite load; a normal white count does not exclude bacterial sepsis.
b: Low parasite density can still cause cerebral malaria
Normal lactate early in shock if sample delayed

faq.q: What is the first drug to give for severe malaria in a child?
faq.a: IV artesunate, because it rapidly reduces parasite load and is safe in children.

faq.q: When should I start a vasopressor?
faq.a: If MAP remains < 65 mmHg after 40 mL/kg fluid bolus and signs of poor perfusion persist.

faq.q: Can I manage a child with severe pneumonia without a ventilator?
faq.a: Only if SpO₂ stays ≥ 90 % on O₂ and work of breathing is mild; otherwise intubation is required.

exam: A 4‑year‑old with malaria presents with a GCS = 7, SpO₂ = 82 % on room air, and a capillary refill of 4 s – what are the immediate priorities? — Secure airway, give 20 mL/kg fluid, start IV artesunate, and prepare for invasive ventilation.

A child with sickle‑cell disease develops chest pain, fever, and new infiltrate on X‑ray – how do you differentiate acute chest syndrome from pneumonia? — Look for sickle‑cell crisis triggers, rapid drop in Hb, and consider exchange transfusion; pneumonia lacks hemolysis.
Why is noradrenaline preferred over dopamine for paediatric shock refractory to fluids? — Noradrenaline has more predictable α‑adrenergic vasoconstriction with less tachyarrhythmia risk.
A patient on high‑flow O₂ still has PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg – what does this indicate and what is the next step? — Hypercapnia shows ventilatory failure; proceed to intubation and controlled ventilation.
What bedside sign suggests early fluid overload in a child on ICU? — Development of peripheral oedema and increasing abdominal girth despite stable vitals.

How would you adjust antibiotic therapy if local data show high resistance to ceftriaxone for Gram‑negative sepsis? — Switch to a carbapenem (e.g., meropenem) if available; otherwise add aminoglycoside coverage.
A child with severe pneumonia has a normal white count – does this rule out bacterial infection? — No; children can have normal or low WCC in severe infection, treat empirically.
When is exchange transfusion indicated in sickle‑cell disease in ICU? — When acute chest syndrome or stroke risk with Hb < 5 g/dL despite fluids, or rapid clinical deterioration.
